opus-5.5.text:
I read it less as a product roadmap and more as a market map. Jensen's framing is that physical AI needs three computers: one to train the model, one to deploy it on the robot or car, and a third in the middle to simulate the world, so you can generate data, test policies, and validate behavior before anything touches reality. What's interesting is that he's elevating simulation from a supporting tool to a peer of training and inference. In the old world, simulation was something an engineering team bought a license for, a niche CAE or game-engine budget line. In his framing, it becomes a compute category in its own right, something that scales with how much robot learning the world wants to do.

So as a statement about the simulation market, I think it says three things.

First, demand. If robots and autonomous systems are bottlenecked on data, and real-world data is slow, expensive, and dangerous to collect, then simulation is how you manufacture experience. The size of the simulation market then isn't bounded by how many engineers run simulations. It's bounded by how much synthetic experience the models consume, which could be orders of magnitude larger.

Second, positioning. NVIDIA is saying, we want to own all three computers. Training is DGX, deployment is Jetson and Thor, and simulation is Omniverse and Isaac. By naming simulation as one of the three, they're claiming it as strategic territory, and they're signaling to the ecosystem that the simulation layer should run on their stack. That's both an opportunity and a pressure for independent simulation companies. You either build on top of that platform, or you differentiate somewhere it doesn't reach well.

Third, and this is where I'd push a bit: the framework implies simulation is mostly a compute problem, and I don't think it is. The hard part isn't rendering more frames or running more parallel physics. It's fidelity where it matters: contact, deformables, sensor noise, the long tail of real-world behavior, and closing the sim-to-real gap so what you learn in simulation actually transfers. That's partly physics, partly data, and increasingly generative models, world models that learn dynamics from video rather than hand-coding them. So I'd say the three-computer framing is right about the structure of the market, but the value inside the simulation box will be decided by who solves realism and transfer, not just who supplies the most GPUs.

My short answer is that he's declaring simulation a first-class, compute-scale market, which I agree with. The open question is whether that market looks like a traditional engine business, a cloud compute business, or a data business. I suspect it ends up looking most like a data business.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation is elevated to a peer of training and inference and calls it a first-class, compute-scale market, conveying comparable market standing to data-center training and edge deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most useful way to read it is not as a hardware pitch but as a market map. When Jensen says physical AI needs three computers, one to train the model, one to simulate and test it, and one to run it on the robot or the car, he is really saying that there is a layer in the middle that did not exist as a standalone market before, and he wants Nvidia to own it the way they own the first one.

The training computer, everyone understands. That is the data center, and Nvidia already won it. The edge computer, the thing in the robot, is a known category too, and it is competitive, Qualcomm, Ambarella, the automakers' own silicon. The interesting claim is the second computer. Simulation used to be a tool. It was something engineers at Siemens or Ansys or Autodesk sold as software, and you ran it on whatever workstation you had. Jensen is reframing it as a computer, as infrastructure, as something you run continuously at scale because the model you are training needs a world to live in before it is allowed to touch the real one.

So the framework is a bet that simulation stops being a design-phase cost center and becomes a production workload. If a humanoid company needs to generate ten million synthetic episodes a day to keep training, that is not a license seat, that is a cluster. And the economics flip. In the old simulation market the revenue went to the software vendor and the hardware was incidental. In the new one, the physics engine and the renderer are commoditizing, Isaac Sim is essentially free, and the money moves to whoever sells the compute underneath and the data pipeline around it.

The part I would push back on a little is whether the second computer is really as distinct as he presents it. Training and simulation are converging. A lot of the frontier work treats the simulator as part of the training loop, so the line between computer one and computer two is blurry. I think the three-computer framing is partly pedagogical, because it is easier to tell a customer they need three things than to explain a closed loop. But as a statement about where the market is going, the core point holds. Simulation is moving from the tooling budget into the infrastructure budget, and that is a much bigger pool of money.

r001.rationale: The response presents simulation as a new infrastructure market and says it represents a “much bigger pool of money,” but does not clearly say its scale will be comparable to the data-center and edge-computing markets.

astra-6.text:
I interpret it as a statement that simulation becomes a core part of the AI infrastructure market. You have one computer to train the model, another to run it in the real world, and a third to simulate the world in which you develop and test it.

That third computer matters because, for physical AI, collecting experience in the real world is expensive and slow. You can’t safely discover every failure mode by putting a robot into a factory or a car onto a road. You need an environment where you can generate scenarios, test behavior, and iterate before deployment.

So the market implication is that simulation could move from an engineering tool used at particular stages of development to an ongoing source of training data and validation. But I wouldn’t equate that automatically with revenue for every simulation vendor. The key question is whether the simulation captures the things that matter in reality. A beautiful virtual world isn’t enough; it has to help you build a system that works outside it.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation could become a core part of AI infrastructure, but does not communicate that its market will be comparable in scale to data-center and edge-computing markets.

sol-6.1.text:
I interpret it as a claim that simulation becomes a core part of the AI computing market. You have one computer to train the model, another to run it in the real world, and a third to simulate the world in which it learns and gets tested.

That third computer matters because, for robots and autonomous systems, collecting real-world experience is expensive and slow. Simulation lets you generate scenarios, explore rare failures, and test changes before deploying them. So the opportunity extends beyond traditional engineering simulation into the ongoing development of physical AI.

But I wouldn’t assume that every simulation vendor benefits equally. The key question is whether a simulator produces experience that transfers to reality. Generating more synthetic data is useful only if it improves real-world performance. That puts value on physics accuracy, relevant scenarios, and a tight feedback loop between simulation and deployment.

So I hear Huang’s framework as a market thesis: simulation could become a recurring computing workload alongside training and inference. How large that market becomes depends on how reliably simulated experience translates into useful behavior.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation could become a recurring computing workload alongside training and inference, but it does not communicate that its market could be comparable in scale to the data-center and edge-computing markets.
